title: Greater Boston Television Corp. v. Federal Communications Commission
lead: A sixteen-year contest for Boston’s Channel 5 repeatedly returned to the Federal Communications Commission after improper contacts tainted an early award. The D.C. Circuit ultimately upheld the Commission’s choice of a new broadcaster while explaining why judicial respect for agency expertise requires a reasoned decision.

actors.name: Federal Communications Commission
actors.role: Federal agency selecting the Channel 5 licensee.

actors.role: Incumbent station owned by the Boston Herald-Traveler’s corporate publisher.

proceedings: After remands concerning improper contacts and an additional comparative hearing, the FCC chose BBI in 1969. D.C. Circuit affirmed; the 1970 opinion was subsequently amended and modified on denial of rehearing in 1971.
limits: The decision concerns WHDH’s unusual licensing history. It did not approve every subsidiary agency rationale, decide the general treatment of ordinary renewals, or certify later broadcast law.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An initial award is reopened because of attempted influence
sections.cue: Temporary broadcasting does not end the comparative contest.
paragraphs: In 1957, the Federal Communications Commission awarded Boston’s Channel 5 license to WHDH, owned by the Boston Herald-Traveler’s corporate publisher. During judicial review, evidence of possible improper contacts between WHDH’s Robert Choate and Commission Chairman McConnaughey prompted an evidentiary remand. While the licensing adjudication was pending, Choate had arranged luncheons and tried to present a proposed legislative amendment affecting media-diversification policy.

A special examiner considered the contacts insufficient to taint the award. The Commission disagreed, finding an attempted pattern of influence. It treated the grant as voidable, rather than void from inception, and proposed setting it aside while permitting temporary operation and reopening the comparison. The court approved that course.

The Commission selected WHDH again in 1962 but limited its license to four months because of its incursions on fair adjudication. When WHDH sought renewal, the Commission opened a designated two-month period for competing applications. Choate died during another appeal. The court remanded to determine the effect of his death and allowed consolidation with the coming comparative proceedings.

sections.title: The examiner favors experience, but the Commission favors a newcomer
sections.cue: The agency explains a different composite judgment.
paragraphs: The new hearing compared WHDH with Boston Broadcasters, Inc., known as BBI, Charles River Civic Television, and Greater Boston Television Corporation. The examiner recommended WHDH. He considered its generally favorable operating record more reliable than newcomers’ promises and believed Choate’s death removed the need for a continuing misconduct disability.

In January 1969 the Commission instead selected BBI. It found WHDH’s performance favorable but average, insufficiently exceptional to earn an affirmative preference. The newcomers offered greater diversification of media control, and BBI proposed greater participation by owners in management. BBI received a slight programming demerit because it inadequately supported an unusually ambitious local-live-program proposal. Charles River received an offsetting demerit because ownership by a charitable foundation might restrict editorializing on legislative questions. Greater Boston failed preliminary requirements involving evaluation of community needs and its antenna site. WHDH also received a demerit for unapproved transfers of de facto control when its president changed.

Four of seven commissioners participated. Three voted for BBI and one for WHDH. Commissioner Johnson expressed little passion between the newcomers but concurred to form a working majority. On reconsideration the Commission distinguished WHDH’s unusual history from ordinary renewal cases. A 1970 policy statement retained renewal protection for solid, substantial public service while excluding unusual cases, often involving judicial remands, in which an incumbent should be compared as a new applicant.

sections.title: The losing applicants challenge both the process and comparison
sections.cue: Judicial scrutiny requires reasons without transferring the licensing choice.
paragraphs: WHDH argued that its license entitled it to ordinary renewal treatment. It characterized use of new-applicant criteria as an unlawful forfeiture and argued that ignoring stability violated due process and legitimate expectations. It also contested diversification and the control-transfer demerit. Charles River challenged the Commission’s vote and BBI’s prospective owner-management integration as unreliable. Greater Boston sought to confine consideration to the earlier record rather than hold a fresh hearing.

Judge Leventhal, writing for Judges Tamm and MacKinnon, described judicial review as enforcing reasonable procedure, substantial evidence, and rational support for ultimate inferences while respecting witness observation and agency expertise. Expertise did not excuse missing reasons. The Commission had to consider material facts and issues, identify crucial facts, articulate reasons, and make comparative findings addressing substantial differences among applicants.

Warning signs could justify intervention when an agency failed to take a hard look or make a reasoned decision. Once it did so, courts should exercise restraint even if they preferred different findings or standards. A discernible path could survive imperfect clarity, and immaterial errors could be harmless, but a reviewing court could not invent missing findings or reasons. Harmless-error treatment required particular care where basic procedural rights were implicated.

sections.title: The Commission’s changed approach survives careful examination
sections.cue: WHDH’s special history supports a fresh contest.
paragraphs: Leventhal described courts and agencies as partners in administration. That relationship demanded articulated standards and reflective findings to restrain whim, improper influence, and irrelevant preferences. An agency changing policy had to show deliberate reconsideration rather than silently disregard earlier standards. The improper contacts, evolving policies, and departure from the examiner justified vigilance here. But the Commission had examined and explained its course. The examiner’s exhaustive work strengthened the record even though the agency rejected his final recommendation; when competing permissible outcomes had substantial support, the Commission made the choice.

The court did not decide whether ordinary renewal applicants could generally lose legitimate expectations or approve the entire 1970 renewal policy. WHDH’s unusual history reasonably justified renewed comparison. The Commission retained latitude to protect adjudication even though the influence was subtle and the chairman rejected the proposed brief. WHDH had not been expressly told it would be judged exactly like a new applicant, but that omission did not limit its opportunity to offer or contest evidence about programming, integration, diversification, past performance, and fitness.

The original misconduct supported reopening competition without either permanently disqualifying WHDH or ignoring what occurred. Choate’s death did not eliminate deterrence concerning associates and investors, although the final comparison imposed no continuing misconduct demerit. WHDH’s actual performance remained relevant; temporary operation simply did not guarantee a lead over stronger newcomers. The four-month license did not make it an ordinary renewal applicant.

sections.title: The remaining objections do not undo the award
sections.cue: Affirmance preserves reservations about subsidiary reasoning.
paragraphs: Diversification was a permissible public-interest criterion because independently selected editorial subjects and reportorial attention mattered even with fairness regulation. The court questioned reliance on the Herald-Traveler’s delay in broadcasting a newspaper scoop, but considered any error minimal in the overall comparison. The control-transfer demerit raised difficult notice and remedy questions; supporting doctrine and its cumulative role made further refinement unnecessary. The court did not validate every such demerit regardless of notice or consequence.

Four participating commissioners constituted a quorum, and three formed a majority. Johnson could vote for BBI to avoid an impasse despite limited enthusiasm; he later rejected reconsideration without reservation. Between BBI and Charles River, owner participation in operation was decisive. The Commission identified six BBI stockholders and their proposed functions, with no finding of insincerity or impracticability. The examiner’s doubts and programming demerit did not require rejection of that separate integration advantage.

The court expressly withheld approval of the reasoning about Charles River’s tax-related editorial restrictions. Authoritative guidance from the Internal Revenue Service and interagency coordination could have helped, but correction would have been minor beside BBI’s strong integration preference. It also rejected Greater Boston’s effort to limit the case to the original record. Substantial evidence supported the selection, and the Commission’s order was affirmed. No judge wrote separately.
